items.readable_text:
Content:
The pigeonhole principle (PHP) is a fundamental fact in combinatorial mathematics. It provides a systematic way to prove various existence statements.

Content:
This principle states the following:

Content:
> If we want to place [MATH: n] items into [MATH: m] containers, where [MATH: n > m,] then at least one container must contain more than one item.

Content:
The above can be illustrated using the following diagram.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/433c3906efef1dca14dcac6428f92090]

Content:
For example, suppose a language school has [MATH: 10] classrooms, and each student is assigned to one of the classrooms. What is the minimum number of students required to guarantee that at least one classroom has at least two students?

Content:
In our case, we have the following:

Content:
- The "items" are the students. Let's denote the number of students by [MATH: n] (unknown).
- The "containers" are classrooms. There are [MATH: 10] classrooms in total.

Content:
The pigeonhole principle guarantees that at least one classroom must have more than one student if [MATH: n>10.] The minimum positive integer that satisfies this condition is [MATH: n=11.]

Content:
Therefore, the minimum number of students required is [MATH: 11.]

sections.normalized_html:
The pigeonhole principle states that if we want to place [MATH: n] items into [MATH: m] containers, where [MATH: n > m,] then at least one container must contain more than one item.

In our case, we have the following:

  • The "items" are the apples. There are [MATH: 39] apples in total.

  • The "containers" are the baskets. Let's denote the number baskets by [MATH: m] (unknown).

The pigeonhole principle guarantees that at least one basket must have more than one apple if [MATH: m<39.] The maximum positive integer that satisfies this condition is [MATH: m=38.]

Therefore, the maximum number of baskets required is [MATH: \bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}38}.]

In our case, we have the following:

  • The "items" are the traffic lights. Let's denote the number of traffic lights by [MATH: n] (unknown).

  • The "containers" are the labels. There are [MATH: 5] labels in total.

By the generalized pigeonhole principle, there is at least one label that has at least [MATH: \left\lceil \frac{n}{5} \right\rceil] traffic lights which got that label.

To ensure that at least [MATH: 7] traffic lights receive the same label, we need [MATH: \left\lceil \frac{n}{5} \right\rceil \geq 7.]

This implies [MATH: \frac{n}{5} > 6.]

Solving for [MATH: n,] we get [MATH: n > 30.]

Since [MATH: n] must be an integer, the minimum value satisfying this condition is [MATH: n = 31 .]

So, the minimum number of of traffic lights required to guarantee that at least [MATH: 7] of traffic lights receive the same label is [MATH: 31.]
